Chapter 2. Developing on Databricks

Databricks has grown significantly in popularity over the past few years, yet many data scientists and ML engineers still struggle to find an effective way to develop their code within the platform.

Notebooks are first-class citizens in Databricks and are widely used by data scientists during the experimentation phase. They are excellent tools for iterative development, and they have helped popularize interactive Python workflows. However, notebooks were not designed to promote best software engineering practices, and code written during experimentation often requires substantial refactoring before it can be deployed to production.

This refactoring typically involves the following:

  • Creating functions, classes, and modules

  • Separating tasks into logical components

  • Isolating configurations that may evolve over time

  • Adding unit tests

  • Implementing logging and documentation

  • Packaging the project’s code

Throughout my career, I have often seen data scientists rely on ML engineers to carry out these steps. This dependency often slows down the path to production, even though much of this rework could be avoided if code were written with production in mind from the outset.

I believe data scientists should be empowered to write production-ready code themselves (while they still can use notebooks), and one of the main goals of this book is to demonstrate how to do this. Despite Databricks’ growing adoption, there is still a lack of best practices tailored to its unique development environment.

Developing on Databricks relies heavily on clusters, and you need to understand the impact of cluster selection. Therefore, before diving into development workflows, let’s briefly review the different types of clusters that are available in Databricks.

Cluster Configurations on Databricks

I’ll start by showing you how to set up an all-purpose cluster for connecting from a local environment or running notebooks within the Databricks workspace. Then, I’ll walk you through the serverless compute option, which allows anyone to run the code using Databricks Free Edition. All code examples are compatible with both cluster types. In Chapter 1, I explained when and why you might choose serverless over classic compute and vice versa.

All-Purpose and Jobs Compute Configuration

Before we start developing on Databricks, we need to set up a cluster. All-purpose clusters are mainly used for development, while you should use jobs clusters to run Lakeflow jobs. Cluster configurations for both all-purpose and jobs clusters are similar, so I’ll just go over the all-purpose cluster settings. You can set up an all-purpose cluster using an API or Terraform, but the easiest way to view the possible configurations of the cluster is via the user interface (UI) located in the compute tab.

Figure 2-1 shows the recommended configurations of the cluster you can follow through the code accompanying this book. The specific configuration settings you should set are as follows:

Policy

Set this to Personal Compute.

Databricks runtime

Set this to 17.3 LTS.

Preferred node type

Select 16 GB Memory, which is one of the smallest sufficient nodes. It is a single-node cluster without any autoscaling policy.

Terminate after _____ minutes of activity

Set this to 30 minutes to reduce costs.

Tags

Set whatever tags you’ll need to make sure development costs can be tracked back to the project.

Let’s go through all the different components of the cluster configurations you can choose from.

Policies and access modes

When creating a cluster, you can choose from the following default policies (unless more policies are created by workspace admins):

Personal Compute

This is ideal for creating single-node compute resources assigned to individual users with minimal setup.

Shared Compute

This is suitable for creating larger, multinode resources shared among users.

Power User Compute

This is an upgraded version of Personal Compute that allows for multinode setup and is designed for distributed single-user workloads.

Unrestricted

This allows full access to all compute configurations when setting up new compute resources.

By default, only workspace admins can create clusters with Shared, Power User, and Unrestricted compute policies. They can grant individual users or user groups access to compute policies. Workspace admins can also create dedicated compute policies, which can be handy if you need to pre-install libraries or restrict cluster creation.

You also need to pay attention to the access modes: Dedicated (formerly Single), Standard (formerly Shared), and No Isolation Shared. Different modes have different limitations. For example, you need to put init script locations and wheel locations in ALLOW_LIST to use them in standard access mode. Check out the documentation for details.

Overall, for ML workflows, I recommend using Dedicated access mode.

Runtime versions

Databricks Runtime is the set of software artifacts that run on Databricks clusters. It defines the environment where your code runs. The pyt version must match the Python version of your project (in our case, Python 3.12).

In this book, I am using Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS, which is, at the moment of writing this book, the latest long-term support (LTS) runtime. For production, it is a common organizational practice to only use LTS runtimes: the support cycle for them is three years. Databricks provides an overview of LTS runtimes and their end-of-support dates. For instance, the end-of-support date for Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS is October 2028.

The runtime comes with a pre-set system environment. These are the specifications of the environment for the Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS:

  • Operating system: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS

  • Java: Zulu17.58+21-CA

  • Scala: 2.13.16

  • Python: 3.12.3

  • R: 4.4.2

  • Delta Lake: 4.0.0

In addition to the pre-set environment, runtimes contain pre-installed Python libraries. That does not mean you have to use the exact versions of the libraries in the runtime. You can also install another version of the library you need, but keep in mind that you are not installing it in a fresh environment, which makes it challenging to reproduce the same environment locally.

Photon acceleration

Photon is Databricks’ native vectorized query engine, and it’s designed to accelerate Spark SQL workloads and DataFrame API calls. It replaces parts of the traditional Spark execution engine with highly optimized code that takes advantage of modern CPU architectures. While enabling Photon increases the DBU rate per hour, it often reduces total cost per workload because jobs complete significantly faster.

However, Photon only accelerates Spark operations and has no effect on single-node Python libraries. A typical ML training script that uses the scikit-learn library operates on Pandas or Polars DataFrames that are loaded into the driver’s memory. Since these libraries bypass Spark entirely, enabling Photon provides no performance benefit for the training step itself.

My advice: enable Photon for data preprocessing tasks that use PySpark (joins, aggregations, and feature transformations at scale), then disable it for compute that runs single-node ML training. This gives you the speed benefits where they matter while avoiding unnecessary DBU costs during training.

Worker and driver nodes

In a single-node setup, you do not have an option to set up worker and driver nodes. You can only choose the size of the single node that acts as both master and worker node. If your task involves running Python code that does not require Spark’s distributed computing capabilities, you need a single-node compute. You may also need a large single-node cluster if the data you are working with is large.

If your task involves large-scale data processing or distributed ML, you need a multinode setup. You can choose different worker and driver node sizes, depending on your task, and set autoscaling policies if you expect that the data you work with may increase in size. It is crucial to choose the right size for your nodes and the right amount of worker nodes, and you also need to choose proper autoscaling policies since they have a big impact on costs.

Advanced settings

In the advanced settings of the cluster, you can do the following:

  • Set up environment variables (e.g., referencing secrets stored in a secret scope)

  • Define init scripts

  • Specify a Docker image to initialize your cluster

  • Specify a logging location

Cost tracking

You can also track cluster-related costs by applying custom tags to a cluster. These tags are propagated to the underlying cloud provider, and you can use them for cost allocation and reporting. To obtain a complete view of infrastructure spend, you should combine Databricks billing data from system tables with cost data from the cloud provider.

Serverless Compute

When it comes to the all-purpose or jobs compute clusters, users have a lot of freedom to adjust configurations as they wish. But this comes with a cost: it will take time for them to find the perfect cluster configuration for their project (and even different cluster configurations for each task).

You can use serverless compute for both development purposes and running a Databricks job. Even though serverless compute may not be sufficient for machine learning model training pipelines, you could still use it for data preprocessing pipelines.

Unlike all-purpose or job compute, we cannot choose the runtime for serverless compute. Instead, we can curate an environment for dependencies. While the concept of an environment and a runtime are similar, environments are much more lightweight.

Serverless environments

In our project, we use Python 3.12, which means we also need to have an environment that supports that Python version. In this book, we use serverless environment version 4, which comes with the following configurations:

  • Operating system: Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS

  • Python: 3.12.3

  • Databricks Connect: 17

  • Scala: 2.13.16

  • JDK: 17

Similar to runtimes, serverless environments come with pre-installed libraries. However, the library versions differ slightly between serverless environment 4 and Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS. This is something to watch out for if your workflows switch between serverless and classic compute, as subtle version mismatches can cause unexpected behavior. I recommend installing your own versions of the libraries you need, to ensure consistency across environments.

Like runtimes, environments have a support cycle of three years. The end-of-support date for environment 4 is in August 2028. You can check out the release notes for the full overview.

Cost tracking

While you can track the costs of classic compute clusters with tags, you would use usage policies for serverless compute. Serverless usage policies consist of tags that are applied to any serverless compute activity incurred by users assigned to the policy. These tags are recorded in system tables, so they let you attribute serverless usage to specific budgets.

Usage policies can be created programmatically, or you can create them through the UI (see Figure 2-2). You can also assign permissions to individual users or user groups (see Figure 2-3). It’s also important to note that if you don’t specify a usage policy ID when using serverless resources, the first available policy (in alphabetical order) assigned to the user will be automatically applied.

Project Setup

In this section, I will walk you through the dataset used in the MLOps part of the book and the different ways you can execute the project’s code.

The book repository can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/mvechtomova/oreilly-mlops-with-databricks. First of all, you should fork the repository so you can go through the next chapters. The repository contains the following folders: mlops (which covers Chapters 2 through 6) and llmops (which covers Chapters 7 through 9).

For now, we’ll talk about the mlops folder, which is structured into the following subfolders and files:

notebooks/

This folder contains notebooks used in different chapters.

scripts/

This folder contains Python scripts that are executed as part of the Databricks job.

databricks.yml

This is the file the Databricks job is defined in.

pyproject.toml

This file contains the Python package definition for the project.

project_config.yml

This file contains isolated configurations of the project, such as the location of the data, model hyperparameters, and model features. In other words, it captures the settings we expect to change during the project’s lifecycle, to ensure that they remain flexible and not hard-coded into the codebase.

src

This folder contains packaged code for the project.

data

This folder contains the required data for the project.

tests

This folder contains unit tests.

version.txt

This file contains a version number that is used for Python package versioning.

First, let’s discuss the dataset in the data folder.

The Dataset

In Chapters 2 through 6, we use the Hotel Booking Cancellation Prediction dataset from Kaggle.1 The dataset contains various features related to bookings, the number of week and weekend nights, the time between arrival and the reservation date, types of meals, whether guests requested parking, room types, and other features. We will use these features to predict the price of a room per night.

This is a dataset that is close to a real-life scenario. In Chapters 3 through 5, we will work on the following scenarios:

Model Serving

This is real-time inference in which all the features required for model prediction are provided by the user.

Model Serving with feature lookup

This is real-time inference in which some features come from the user and others are retrieved from a feature store. In this case, the model computes the predicted price per night in real time, using the full feature set.

Feature Serving

This is real-time retrieval in which the predicted price per night is precomputed in a batch process and stored in a feature store. At serving time, the user only provides a booking ID, which is used to fetch the stored prediction.

In the project_config.yml file, I specified the target and features that will be used for model training. Our configuration file is relatively simple; for more complex projects with hierarchical configurations, it’s worth checking out the Hydra project.

You’ll also notice the usage_policy_id parameter. We created the usage policy in the section “Cost tracking”, and I’m including it here so you can pass the usage policy when provisioning serverless resources (such as a Model Serving endpoint). This will allow you to properly attribute and track costs associated with those resources:

dev:
 catalog: mlops_dev
 schema: hotel_booking

acc:
 catalog: mlops_acc
 schema: hotel_booking

prd:
 catalog: mlops_prd
 schema: hotel_booking

parameters:
 learning_rate: 0.05
 n_estimators: 200
 max_depth: 3

num_features:
 - number_of_adults
 - number_of_children
 - number_of_weekend_nights
 - number_of_week_nights
 - car_parking_space
 - special_requests
 - lead_time

cat_features:
 - type_of_meal
 - room_type
 - arrival_month
 - market_segment_type

target: average_price

usage_policy_id: cdad6f29-a213-4525-9330-e25b90afbe7a

Next, the project_config.yml file contains model hyperparameters, plus catalogs and schemas used in different environments. You can also update this file to put in your own schema and catalog names if you wish. For now, we’ll only focus on the development environment; we’ll discuss other environments and deployment strategies in Chapter 5.

We will also get to hyperparameter tuning in Chapter 3, where we’ll discuss how we can use MLflow to log all the metrics and parameters and how we got to the parameters specified in the file. It is a common approach to do periodic retraining with the same hyperparameters (as hyperparameter tuning is quite costly) and only perform fine-tuning when there are signs of performance degradation.

Python Tooling

Most people in the industry are convinced that we need to start packaging the code. But what is the right way? What tools should we use?

The Python ecosystem has changed significantly over the last several years, starting around 2016. Before that, everyone was using setup.py together with requirements.txt, plus the following set of tools:

venv or virtualenv

They used these for virtual environment management. The venv tool is shipped with Python 3, and virtualenv is a package maintained by Python Packaging Authority (PyPa).

pip

They used this for package management.

setuptools

They used this for build backend.

twine

They used this for package publishing.

In data analytics and data science, conda was a popular choice. This was a result of the efforts of an organization called Anaconda that was founded in 2012 by Peter Wang and Travis Oliphant,2 with the goal of bringing Python into business data analytics. The conda tool is a multipurpose tool that assists with package, virtual environment, and Python version management. It is worth mentioning that in 2024, Anaconda introduced changes in licensing that forced conda users to look for alternatives.

In 2016, the PEP 518 standard was introduced, and it specified that build system dependencies should be stored in a pyproject.toml file. In 2020, PEP 621 was introduced, and it defined how project metadata should be stored in the pyproject.toml file.

Between 2017 and 2020, multiple projects started using pyproject.toml to serve multiple purposes and try to eliminate the need to have so many tools. The best-known projects were hatch, poetry,3 and pdm.

In 2023, Rust started taking over the Python ecosystem due to its speed, and another multipurpose tool called Rye was released. In February 2024, another Rust-based tool called uv developed by Astral entered the market, and it has won the hearts of the Python community since then. Astral also took over the development and maintenance of Rye.

The uv tool is, in my opinion, by far the most intuitive tool to use, and it is blazingly fast. It is therefore the tool I will be using in this book.4 You should follow the official installation instructions to install uv.

The pyproject.toml file

Let’s walk through the sections of the pyproject.toml file we will use for the MLOps project.

Project section

In the project section of the pyproject.toml file, we specify the Python version and all the project dependencies: 

[project]
name = "hotel-booking"
dynamic = ["version"]
description = "Code accompanying MLOps with Databrick O'Reilly book"
requires-python = ">=3.12, <3.13"
dependencies = [
   "mlflow==3.11.1",
   "cffi==1.17.1",
   "cloudpickle==3.1.1",
   "numpy==2.4.0",
   "pandas==2.3.0",
   "pyarrow==22.0.0",
   "databricks-sdk==0.102.0",
   "scikit-learn==1.7.0",
   "lightgbm==4.6.0",
   "scipy==1.16.0",
   "pydantic==2.11.7",
   "loguru==0.7.3",
   "python-dotenv==1.1.1",
   "ray[tune]==2.52.1",
   "optuna==4.4.0",
   "sdv==1.24.0",
   "databricks-feature-engineering==0.14.0",
   "databricks-feature-lookup==1.11.0"
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = ["databricks-connect>=17.3.2, <18",
      "ipykernel>=6.29.5, <7",
      "pip>=25.0.1, <26",
      "pre-commit>=4.1.0, <5",
      "pytest>=8.3.4, <9",
      "pytest-mock>=3.14.0, <4"]

ci = ["databricks-connect>=17.3.2, <18",
     "pre-commit>=4.1.0, <5",
     "pytest>=8.3.4, <9",
     "pytest-mock>=3.14.0, <4"]

First of all, it is important to note that we use Python 3.12, which matches the Python version of the Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS runtime and environment version 4 for serverless.

Secondly, all the package dependencies are pinned to very specific versions. While this may seem beneficial at first glance, it is not considered best practice for packages that are intended to be reused across multiple projects, as strict version pinning can easily lead to dependency conflicts. So for reusable packages, it is generally recommended to define a supported range of Python versions and dependency versions instead. In this case, however, the Python package is not designed for reuse; it simply serves as a convenient way to define and manage project-level dependencies.

When you’re installing the package, you don’t need to manually specify all dependency versions listed in the pyproject.toml file. These dependencies are included in the package metadata and will be installed automatically as part of the package installation process.

Optional dependencies are also defined in the pyproject.toml file, and you can install them when you need them for development purposes or for tests to run in a CI pipeline, for example. Note that they will not be installed automatically when the package itself is added as a dependency, as they are not included in package metadata.

Build-system section

The build-system section of the pyproject.toml file specifies the build backend that is used to package and distribute the project. In this case, we are using setuptools as the build backend, and the package version is dynamically determined based on the contents of the version.txt file.

While several alternative build backends are available, such as build backend provided by uv, or Hatchling, setuptools remains the most mature and widely supported backend in the Python ecosystem:

[build-system]
requires = [
 "setuptools>=72.0"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where =["src"]
include = ["hotel_booking*"]

[tool.setuptools.dynamic]
version = { file = "version.txt" }

Linting and formatting

For linting and formatting, we use Ruff, which is the fastest tool out there for this purpose. It was developed by Astral and written in Rust. Just like uv, it won the hearts of the Python community and replaced the functionality of many other tools. Configurations for Ruff are specified in the tool section of the pyproject.toml file:

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 90

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = [
   "F",    # pyflakes rules
   "E",    # pycodestyle error rules
   "W",    # pycodestyle warning rules
   "B",    # flake8-bugbear rules
   "I",    # isort rules
   "UP",   # pyupgrade rules
   "SIM",  # flake8-simplify rules
   "ERA",  # eradicate rules
   "C",    # pylint convention rules
   "ANN"   # flake8-annotations rules
]
ignore = [
   "D107", # Missing docstring in `__init__`
   "D203", # incorrect-blank-line-before-class
   "D213", # multi-line-summary-second-line
   "C901", # too complex
   "ERA001", # commented out code
]

[tool.ruff.format]
indent-style = "space"

These configurations are also used for pre-commit hooks that should be installed locally to enforce the rules. Pre-commit hooks are defined in the .pre-commit-config.yaml file:

exclude: ^tests/resources/
repos:
 - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
   rev: v6.0.0
   hooks:
     - id: check-added-large-files
     - id: check-json
     - id: check-toml
     - id: check-yaml
     - id: end-of-file-fixer
     - id: trailing-whitespace
 - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
   rev: v0.15.1
   hooks:
     - id: ruff
       args: [--fix, --exit-non-zero-on-fix, --show-fixes]
     - id: ruff-format

To make pre-commit hooks execute on every commit, install them with the pre-commit install command. To ensure all the files follow the predefined rules, run the uv run pre-commit run –all-files command as part of the CI pipeline.

Pytest configurations

The pyproject.toml file can also contain some pytest configurations that allow it to run tests without running into errors, and for that reason, we must specify the testpaths and pythonpath configurations:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "-s --no-header --no-summary"
testpaths = [ "tests" ]
pythonpath = [ "." ]

Now that we’ve gone through the pyproject.toml file and the dataset, let’s take a deep dive into the code.

Project Code: Data Preprocessing

You can find the chapter2_preprocess_data.py script in the notebooks folder. Note that for the code to run, you must either create a catalog and a schema with the name specified in the project_config.yml file under the dev key or update the file with the catalog name and schema name you prefer to use instead.

First of all, we create a Spark session and load the project configuration:

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

from hotel_booking.config import ProjectConfig

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

cfg = ProjectConfig.from_yaml("../project_config.yml")
catalog = cfg.catalog
schema = cfg.schema

We use the ProjectConfig class from the config module of our custom hotel_booking package. This class is built on Pydantic, which provides robust data validation to ensure that all configuration values match the expected data types.

Beyond basic type checking, Pydantic supports enforcement of additional constraints, such as value ranges, allowed patterns (e.g., regular expressions), and custom validation rules. This helps catch configuration errors early by enforcing these rules at runtime, so misconfigurations will fail fast with clear error messages, instead of causing subtle bugs later in the pipeline.

In the following example, we enforce an opinionated valid value range for hyperparameters by using Pydantic’s Field() validator. Specifically, we use parameters such as gt (greater than) and le (less than or equal to) to define acceptable bounds for the field’s value:

import yaml
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field


class Parameters(BaseModel):
   """Model training hyperparameters with validation."""

   learning_rate: float = Field(gt=0, le=0.2)
   n_estimators: int = Field(ge=10, le=10000)
   max_depth: int = Field(ge=1, le=50)


class ProjectConfig(BaseModel):
   """Project configuration parameters loaded from project_config.yml."""

   model_config = ConfigDict(protected_namespaces=())

   num_features: list[str]
   cat_features: list[str]
   target: str
   catalog: str
   schema: str
   parameters: Parameters
   usage_policy_id: str

   @classmethod
   def from_yaml(
       cls: "ProjectConfig",
       config_path: str,
       env: str = "dev") -> "ProjectConfig":
       """Load and parse configuration settings from a YAML file.

       :param config_path: Path to the YAML configuration file
       :param env: Environment name to load environment-specific settings
       :return: ProjectConfig instance initialized with parsed configuration
       """
       if env not in ["prd", "acc", "dev"]:
           raise ValueError(
               f"Invalid environment: {env}. Expected 'prd', 'acc', or 'dev'"
           )

       with open(config_path) as f:
           config_dict = yaml.safe_load(f)
       config_dict["catalog"] = config_dict[env]["catalog"]
       config_dict["schema"] = config_dict[env]["schema"]
       for k in ["dev", "acc", "prd"]:
           config_dict.pop(k)
       return cls(**config_dict)

Before we proceed, we need to make sure the catalog and schema exist and, if not, create them:

spark.sql(f"CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS {catalog}")
spark.sql(f"CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS {catalog}.{schema}")

After we create the Spark session, load the configuration, and make sure catalog and schema exist, we load and clean the data (note the dataset-specific cleaning commands) and store the result in a Delta table.5 Also note that we enable C⁠h⁠a⁠n⁠g⁠e​D⁠a⁠t⁠a⁠F⁠e⁠e⁠d to track all row-level changes between versions of the Delta table:

from datetime import datetime

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("../data/booking.csv")
df.columns = df.columns.str.replace(r"[ -]", "_", regex=True)
df["date_of_reservation"] = df["date_of_reservation"].apply(
   lambda x: "3/1/2018" if x == "2018-2-29" else x
)
df["date_of_reservation"] = df["date_of_reservation"].apply(
   lambda x: datetime.strptime(x, "%m/%d/%Y")
)
df["arrival_date"] = df["date_of_reservation"] + pd.to_timedelta(
   df["lead_time"], unit="d"
)
df["arrival_month"] = df["arrival_date"].dt.month

dst_table = f"{catalog}.{schema}.hotel_booking"

spark.createDataFrame(df).write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable(f"{dst_table}")

spark.sql(
 f"""ALTER TABLE {dst_table}
  SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true);"""
)

Now that we’ve gone through the code (the full version is available in the notebook), our next step is to run it. Before that, however, it is worth taking a closer look at the Databricks developer tools.

Databricks Developer Tools

There are four main local developer tools Databricks provides: Databricks CLI, Declarative Automation Bundles (DABs), Databricks Connect, and Databricks extension for Visual Studio Code. Let’s go through them one by one.

Databricks CLI

Databricks CLI is a command line interface that allows you to interact with the Databricks platform. It is a very powerful tool with a large range of commands that cover functionality that’s similar to that of Databricks Terraform modules and APIs.

You should use Databricks CLI to authenticate toward Databricks from your local machine. We need to start by installing it, and Databricks provides comprehensive documentation on how to do it on different OS.

Databricks CLI provides multiple authentication options. I do not recommend using personal access tokens, as a leaked token could grant full access to whatever resources you have access to across your Databricks workspace and Unity Catalog, including data, models, jobs, and serving endpoints. Instead, use user-to-machine authentication,6 which relies on short-lived OAuth tokens that expire automatically and do not carry the same risk if intercepted.

For the workspace-level commands, use the following command to authenticate:

databricks auth login --host workspace-url

It creates an authentication profile in the .databrickscfg file that contains the profile name and configurations for the profile. It is also a good practice to use a user-understandable profile name, so that you can pass the -p option when authenticating:

[mlops-book]
host  = https://oreil.ly/DtiuJ
auth_type = databricks-cli

You use the profiles to authenticate with Databricks when you’re using developer tools.

Declarative Automation Bundles

You may have noticed that the repository contains the databricks.yml file. This is the DAB configuration file, which must be located in the root of the bundle project folder.

At their core, DABs enable you to manage Databricks projects through an IaC approach. Using the databricks.yml file, you can define the artifacts and resources your project requires. In Chapter 5, we’ll take a deep dive into specific resources you can deploy using DABs. For now, let’s explore the syntax and core commands.

Syntax of the databricks.yml file

First, every databricks.yml file must contain a bundle section with a name. Optionally, you can specify the Databricks CLI version and information about your source code. You can also provide an interactive cluster_id, which will override any other cluster specifications in the bundle, but this will only work in development mode (which we’ll discuss below). I recommend specifying the cluster_id under the target section for development purposes instead, as follows (note that the cluster_id specification is not relevant for serverless compute):

bundle: # Required.
 name: string # Required.
 databricks_cli_version: string
 cluster_id: string
 git:
   origin_url: string
   branch: string

The artifacts section is where you can specify which packages need to be built as part of the bundle deployment. It can run any build command (for example, uv build) given that the dependency (here, uv) is installed.

For the whl type, you can set the dynamic_version parameter. If you set it to true, a dynamic version with a timestamp will be created. This is an important consideration for jobs that use an interactive cluster, as it ensures that the cluster will use the latest code changes. However, this isn’t necessary for job clusters or serverless clusters, as they handle this behavior automatically:

artifacts:
 some-unique-artifact-identifier:
   build: string
   files:
     - source: string
   path: string
   type: string
   dynamic_version: boolean

You can also set up custom variables directly in the databricks.yml file. Then, you can pass these variables to the deployment by entering the databricks bundle deploy –var command. For traceability purposes, it is a good idea to pass the git_sha variable. We will use this later to tag our experiment runs and models, to ensure that we can always link a model back to the exact version of the code that created it.

You define these variables within a variables section like this:

variables:
 some-unique-variable-name:
   description: string
   default: string or complex

To keep your databricks.yml file clean and maintainable, especially as your project grows, you can move job definitions into separate files and reference them using the include section. This modular approach helps you avoid a single, monolithic configuration file that becomes hard to read and review:

include:
 - 'some-file-or-path-glob-to-include'
 - 'another-file-or-path-glob-to-include'

In the sync section of the databricks.yml file, you can specify what files or directories should be included or excluded from the bundle deployment:

sync:
 include:
   - 'some-file-or-path-glob-to-include'
   - 'another-file-or-path-glob-to-include'
 exclude:
   - 'some-file-or-path-glob-to-exclude'
   - 'another-file-or-path-glob-to-exclude'
 paths:
   - 'some-file-or-path-to-synchronize'

Next, in the resources section of the databricks.yml file, you can define all the resources that should be deployed as part of the bundle. DABs support a wide and continuously expanding set of resource types, including alerts, apps, clusters, dashboards, Lakeflow jobs, and SQL warehouses.7

This is how you define resources in the databricks.yml file:

resources:
 clusters:
   some-unique-programmatic-identifier-for-this-cluster:
     # See the REST API create request payload reference for clusters.
 experiments:
   some-unique-programmatic-identifier-for-this-experiment:
     # See the REST API create request payload reference for experiments.
 apps:
   some-unique-programmatic-identifier-for-this-app:
     # See the REST API create request payload reference for apps.
 jobs:
   some-unique-programmatic-identifier-for-this-job:
     # See the REST API create request payload reference for jobs.
 pipelines:
   some-unique-programmatic-identifier-for-this-pipeline:
     # See the REST API create request payload reference for 
     # Lakeflow declarative pipelines.

In the permissions section, you can specify permissions for all the resources defined in the bundle configuration. You can set permissions for groups, users, or service principals. The allowed top-level permission levels are CAN_VIEW, CAN_MANAGE, and CAN_RUN. You can also specify permissions on the resource level:

permissions:
 - level: <permission-level>
   group_name: <unique-group-name>
 - level: <permission-level>
   user_name: <unique-user-name>
 - level: <permission-level>
   service_principal_name: <unique-principal-name>

The run_as section allows you to specify the identity, such as a service principal, to use to run a job. The user must have CAN_USE permissions for the service principal to use this feature:

run_as:
 service_principal_name: <service-principal-name>

Finally, you can use the targets section to override settings that are specified elsewhere in the databricks.yml file. For development purposes, it is convenient to specify an interactive cluster_id under the dev target and utilize the development mode.

The development mode enables the following behavior:8

  • It adds the [dev ${workspace.current_user.short_name}] prefix to all resource names, and it tags each job with a dev Databricks tag.

  • It allows you to override job clusters (which is not allowed in production mode).

  • It pauses all schedules and triggers.

  • It enables concurrent runs on all deployed jobs and disables the deployment lock for faster iteration.

This is how you can define targets in the databricks.yml file:

targets:
 some-unique-programmatic-identifier-for-this-target:
   artifacts:
     # See the preceding "artifacts" syntax.
   bundle:
     # See the preceding "bundle" syntax.
   cluster_id: string
   default: true | false
   mode: development
   presets:
     preset: value
   resources:
     # See the preceding "resources" syntax.
   sync:
     # See the preceding "sync" syntax.
   variables:
     preceding-unique-variable-name: non-default-value
   workspace:
     # See the preceding "workspace" syntax.
   run_as:
     # See the preceding "run_as" syntax.

It is common practice to define the workspace configuration under a target because workspace-related values, such as the host and authentication details, typically differ by environment.9 The workspace section can contain the following information:

workspace:
 artifact_path: string
 auth_type: string
 file_path: string
 host: string
 profile: string
 root_path: string
 state_path: string

Note that in development mode, the bundle’s root path must be under the user’s home directory, so it is common to have different root_path values for different targets.

Now that we’ve covered the different sections of the databricks.yml file, let’s take a closer look at the version used in this book’s code repository.

The databricks.yml file

In the databricks.yml file, we specify the bundle name first:

bundle:
 name: oreilly-mlops-with-databricks

Then, we define the artifacts to build. In this case, we use the uv build command to create the package wheel, which we can reference later as the task library. The path is “.”, which points to the root of the directory: 

artifacts:
 default:
   type: whl
   build: uv build
   path: .

If you have multiple packages within the same repository, the path will be a folder that contains the pyproject.toml file.

Next, we define the following bundle variables:

git_sha and branch

We will use these later as arguments for our Python tasks, so that we can tag experiment runs and registered models with actual git_sha and branch values.

schedule_pause_status

We can use this to pause the scheduled job when the target is not set to development mode, which is convenient if we use the acc target.

usage_policy_id

We can use this to pass to serverless resources deployed through the bundle for cost allocation. We will discuss this in detail in Chapter 9.

The following example shows how to deploy these bundle variables:

variables:
 git_sha:
   description: git_sha
   default: abcd
 branch:
   description: branch
   default: main
 schedule_pause_status:
   description: schedule pause status
   default: PAUSED
# matches project_config.yml
 usage_policy_id:
   description: usage/budget policy id for cost attribution
   default: cdad6f29-a213-4525-9330-e25b90afbe7a

In the sync section, we specify the dist folder to make sure the built artifacts are easily accessible when running the code on Databricks during the development phase:

sync:
 include:
   - dist/*

Note that we haven’t defined any resources directly in our databricks.yml file. Instead, we’ve created separate YAML files for our jobs and placed them in a resources folder. Here’s how you can include those resources in the bundle definition; make sure there are no irrelevant files in that directory:

include:
 - resources/*

Finally, in the targets section, we define three targets: dev, acc, and prd. The dev target is our default and is used primarily for development. It’s configured to use development mode, which automatically adds the dev ${workspace.current_user.short_name} prefix to all deployed resources and pauses any schedules.

The acc target is intended for acceptance testing, and prd is used for deploying code to production. The following example shows how to deploy these three targets:

targets:
 dev:
   default: true
   mode: development
   workspace:
     host: <your_host>
     root_path: /Workspace/Users/${workspace.current_user.userName}/
                .bundle/${bundle.target}/${bundle.name}
 acc:
   workspace:
     host: <your_host>
     root_path: /Shared/.bundle/${bundle.target}/${bundle.name}
   variables:
     schedule_pause_status: PAUSED

 prd:
   workspace:
     host: <your_host>
     root_path: /Shared/.bundle/${bundle.target}/${bundle.name}
   variables:
     schedule_pause_status: UNPAUSED

In Chapter 5, we’ll take a closer look at these environments and explore how to promote code among them.

Now that we’ve gone through the databricks.yml file, let’s take a closer look at how we can interact with automation bundles.

Using DABs

Before we go into details, you need to make sure that the host defined in the target matches the Databricks profile you use to log in to Databricks. If you’ve forked the repository and cloned it to your local machine, make sure to update the host value in the databricks.yml file. Without this change, you won’t be able to run the code examples covered in the following sections.

There are four main Databricks CLI commands related to DABs:

databricks bundle validate

This checks whether your databricks.yml file is configured correctly.

databricks bundle deploy

This deploys the resources defined in your databricks.yml file.

databricks bundle run <job resource name>

This executes the specified job.

databricks bundle destroy

This removes all the assets that were created by the bundle.

After the databricks bundle deploy command is executed, all the project files and built artifacts are uploaded to the root_path location specified under target. There, you’ll find the following:

The artifacts folder

This holds the Python wheel files that were built for the project.

The files folder

This contains all your project’s source files.

The state folder

This stores the Terraform state of the bundle.10

The resources folder

This contains the direct deployment state file.

It’s important to pay attention to authentication when using DABs, specifically the evaluation order:

  1. For any command run from the bundle working directory , evaluate and authenticate the values of fields within a project’s bundle setting files.

  2. Evaluate and authenticate the values of environment variables (DATABRICKS_HOST and DATABRICKS_TOKEN).

  3. Evaluate and authenticate the configuration profile field values within the .databrickscfg file.

Note that if you happen to have an environment variable set up, it may mess up authentication.

Databricks Connect

Databricks Connect is a Python package that allows you to trigger an execution of PySpark code on a Databricks cluster from a local environment.

Before we proceed, you need to make sure that the host mentioned in the profile configuration has an active all-purpose cluster that matches the specifications we mentioned earlier, when we went through the all-purpose cluster configuration. Alternatively, you can use serverless.

We have already gone through the pyproject.toml setup and uv. Now, you need to create a virtual environment that you can activate later. To do this, from the project folder in a terminal, you can run the uv sync command as follows:

uv sync --extra dev #You can also run an alternative command if you use Windows.

source .venv/bin/activate 

python

Note that you need to use Python 3.12 and Databricks Connect version 17.3.x,  to match the runtime. With the Python command, you get into the Python console, and then, you can run the following commands using a serverless cluster: 

from databricks.connect import DatabricksSession

spark = DatabricksSession.builder.profile(
    "mlops-book").serverless(True).getOrCreate()

df = spark.read.table("samples.nyctaxi.trips")

df.show(5)

Alternatively, you can use an interactive cluster by providing the cluster ID.

Spark commands will run on a Databricks cluster.

There are a couple of things to pay attention to here:

  • You need to choose the correct profile from the .databrickscfg file. If the profile is named DEFAULT, it is not needed.

  • You’ll use DatabricksSession to run Spark code. If you, for example, run df.toPandas(),  which you may need for an ML library you are using, the dataframe will be loaded into your machine’s memory. And if the data is too big, you will get out-of-memory errors.

It may be surprising, but you can import PySpark, even though PySpark is not listed as a dependency of Databricks Connect and uv does not show that PySpark is installed. You can see this if you try to install Databricks Connect in a clean virtual environment as follows:

(test) mariavechtomova@Mac test % uv pip install databricks-connect==17.3.5
Resolved 30 packages in 293ms
Prepared 8 packages in 593ms
Installed 30 packages in 301ms
  + certifi==2026.1.4|
  + cffi==2.0.0
  + charset-normalizer==3.4.4|
  + cryptography==46.0.5|
  + databricks-connect==17.3.5|
  + databricks-sdk==0.89.0|
  + google-auth==2.48.0
  + googleapis-common-protos==1.72.0|
  + grpcio==1.78.0|
  + grpcio-status==1.78.0|
  + idna==3.11|
  + numpy==2.4.2
  + packaging==26.0
  + pandas==2.3.3
  + protobuf==6.33.5
  + Py4J==0.10.9.9
  + pyarrow==23.0.1
  + pyasn1==0.6.2
  + pyasn1-modules==0.4.2|
  + pycparser==3.0
  + python-dateutil==2.9.0.post@
  + pytz==2025.2
  + requests==2.32.5
  + rsa==4.9.1|
  + setuptools==82.0.0
  + six==1.17.0
  + typing-extensions==4.15.0|
  + tzdata==2025.3|
  + urllib3==2.6.3
  + zstandard==0.25.0

This is because PySpark is “hidden” and embedded into Databricks Connect—which is why it’s a bad idea to list both Databricks Connect and PySpark in your project dependencies. You can view PySpark in this “hidden” location by going to .venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages as follows:

(test) mariavechtomova@Mac site-packages % ls -la | grep pyspark
drwxr-xI-x@ 56 mariavechtomova staff      1792 Feb 18 00:23 pyspark

If you try to use SparkSession instead of DatabricksSession, however, it would not work because it misses necessary context, as shown here:

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()
df = spark.read.table("samples.nyctaxi.trips")
df.show(5)

In this case, import works without issues because PySpark is part of Databricks Connect. However, when you try to run the second line, you will get the following error message:

RuntimeError: “Only remote Spark sessions using Databricks Connect are supported. Use
DatabricksSession.builder to create a remote Spark session instead.”

The same command does work in the Databricks extension for Visual Studio Code, however, because the extension automatically injects the required connection details through a .databricks.env file it creates inside the .databricks folder of your project. It contains the following environment variables:

  • DATABRICKS_AUTH_TYPE

  • DATABRICKS_BUNDLE_TARGET

  • DATABRICKS_HOST

  • DATABRICKS_METADATA_SERVICE_URL

  • DATABRICKS_PROJECT_ROOT

  • DATABRICKS_SERVERLESS_COMPUTE_ID

  • PROFILE

  • PYDEVD_WARN_SLOW_RESOLVE_TIMEOUT

  • SPARK_CONNECT_PROGRESS_BAR_ENABLED

  • SPARK_CONNECT_USER_AGENT

Databricks Extension for Visual Studio Code

The Databricks extension for Visual Studio Code integrates with all other developer tools: Databricks CLI, DABs, and Databricks Connect.11 This makes it very easy to connect to the Databricks workspace and execute your code using a Databricks cluster.

Since this is a monolithic repository (monorepo) setup, I highly recommend installing the Python Envy VS Code extension,12 which will automatically detect the virtual environment based on the file you have opened.

After you’ve installed the extension, follow these steps:

  1. Open the project; make sure to choose the mlops folder of the repository as the local folder, as shown in Figure 2-4).

  2. Run the cd mlops & uv sync –extra dev command to sync dependencies and make sure that the .venv virtual environment has been created.

  3. Select an interpreter using Python extension (or it will be automatically selected if Python Envy VS Code extension is installed)

  4. Make sure the databricks.yml file in the mlops folder contains the host that matches the host of the profile that was created earlier.

  5. Authenticate using the same profile.

  6. Select the cluster that you created earlier or choose the serverless compute option.

In the end, Remote Folder must be present under CONFIGURATION and the Active Environment and Databricks Connect sections must have checkmarks next to them (see Figure 2-4).

Now, let’s create a demo.py file (the same code we tried to run from a terminal) and add # Databricks notebook source so that the code can be recognized as a notebook (see Figure 2-5). The cells are delimited by a line containing # COMMAND ----------.13

We can run the code interactively by clicking Run Cell. We can also execute project code (for example, notebooks/chapter2_preprocess_data.py) from VS Code in a similar way.

However, some code can only run in a Databricks environment. For example, the databricks-feature-engineering package is not supported locally, and some Delta table commands will fail outside Databricks. Secondly, even if you use PySpark for preprocessing, most ML libraries require Pandas (or sometimes Polars) DataFrames as input for training. Both Pandas and Polars compute on a single node, which means that even in a Databricks environment, you are not directly leveraging the distributed power of Spark. The advantage of using them, however, is that you can attach your notebook to a larger cluster with more memory. If you run the same code locally, it will use your laptop’s memory, and you can’t easily scale that up.

Let’s explore how to make notebooks available in the Databricks workspace and execute them there instead.

The Databricks extension for Visual Studio Code allows you to sync the entire project to the workspace. To do this, click the Sync button in the Remote Folder tab on the screen shown previously in Figure 2-4, and the extension will run the databricks sync <folder> /Users/<user_name>/<folder> --watch command in the background. As a result, any local changes you make will be automatically reflected in the workspace without you having to perform manual synchronization.

You can also use this approach to make a wheel file for your project available in the workspace. Simply run the uv build command, and the wheel you generate will be synced along with the rest of the files (unless you add the wheel location to the .gitignore file).

It is important to note that the databricks sync command provides one-way synchronization. Changes made directly in the Databricks workspace are not reflected locally, and any subsequent sync will overwrite workspace code.

Alternatively, you can make the code accessible in the workspace by using the Git folder functionality. After creating a Git folder, you can authenticate by linking your Git account to Databricks or by using a personal access token from GitHub or another supported version control provider. Git folders enable bidirectional synchronization, which means changes made in notebooks can be pushed back to Git (although this may become inconvenient when dealing with merge conflicts). In addition, managing project dependencies through Git Folders can be challenging.

Finally, you can use the databricks bundle deploy command to make all project files available in the workspace together with the built artifact, which is the main advantage this approach has over syncing. (Make sure to run the command from the mlops folder that contains the databricks.yml file.) However, this method also provides one-way synchronization. Note that using the sync command together with bundle deploy may corrupt the bundle state.

Running Code in a Databricks Notebook

You may have noticed that the chapter2_preprocess_data.py script is also just a Python file (not an IPython notebook with the .ipynb extension) that has #Databricks notebook source as the first line and that the cells are delimited by # COMMAND ----------.

Let’s assume we used the databricks bundle deploy command, which makes this notebook available under the files folder in the bundle root in the workspace. Figure 2-6 shows what the notebook looks like if we open it.

To run a Databricks notebook, you need to select a cluster and install the project package. Let’s see how you can do this for serverless and all-purpose compute.

Using serverless compute

When using serverless compute, you must choose an environment before proceeding. In the example in Figure 2-7, we select a Base environment of Standard v4 and install the custom package wheel that was built together with the bundle (which is available under the bundle root in the artifacts/.internal folder). Notice that we selected the mlops_usage_policy here so that the costs related to project development will be attributed correctly.

Since selecting an environment is a manual process, developers may forget to choose one. Therefore, you can configure a default custom base environment for serverless compute to ensure that the correct environment is applied to the project.

This environment will be automatically applied to all notebooks when serverless compute is selected. The following env_v4.yaml file will be uploaded to /Volumes/mlops_dev/utils/envs/:

environment_version: "4"
dependencies:
 - mlflow==3.11.1
 - numpy==2.4.0
 - pandas==2.3.0
 - pyarrow==22.0.0
 - databricks-sdk==0.102.0
 - scikit-learn==1.7.0
 - lightgbm==4.6.0
 - scipy==1.16.0
 - pydantic==2.11.7

Figure 2-8 demonstrates how a workspace admin (who will have the necessary permissions) can set this environment as the workspace base environment via the Workspace Compute settings. The Compute settings also allow you to configure a default package repository, which is useful when your organization uses JFrog or another private package repository.

Using all-purpose compute

If serverless compute does not satisfy your development needs, then you can always opt for all-purpose compute. Earlier in the chapter, we went through configuration of all-purpose compute. We can create a cluster with these specifications, meaning that we will be using Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS (which is close to environment 4 in terms of its operating system, Python version, and installed packages).

Much like how you installed a custom library in the serverless environment, you can install it on an all-purpose cluster. The custom package wheel is built together with the bundle, and you can find it under the bundle root in the artifacts/.internal folder (see Figure 2-9).14

If the custom package has dependencies hosted in a private package repository, you need to make sure that the default package repository is configured in the Compute settings.

We have already gone through the options for making sure that custom dependencies are available in the notebook for both serverless and all-purpose compute options. However, this is not an interactive way to develop, especially if you want to change the modules in your package. Also, we have assumed that we’ve been using the bundle deploy option—but what if we used Git folders instead?

To install specific libraries across all nodes of a cluster from a Databricks notebook, you can also use the %pip install command. This allows you to install them from PyPi, a private repository, or a wheel located in the workspace or a volume.

You can also install all the project dependencies specified in the pyproject.toml file by running the pip install -e . command and restarting Python with the dbutils.library.restartPython() command. To make the project itself importable, you also need to run the following code to adjust the path, which is considered a bad development practice:

from pathlib import Path
import sys

sys.path.append(str(Path.cwd().parent / 'src'))

However, this is necessary in this example because our package code is under the src folder.

Overall, developing directly in a Databricks notebook is not my first choice. Notebooks make it difficult to structure code into modules, run tests, and apply consistent formatting. However, to be 100% sure that the code works as intended, you ultimately need to execute it in a Databricks environment.

However, you cannot fully reproduce the same environment you have on Databricks locally—you can only achieve an approximation (as we did earlier). This is because the Databricks Runtime is curated and preconfigured with a set of installed libraries. When additional dependencies are installed on top of it, the resulting dependency tree may differ from what you have locally. Installing all runtime libraries locally would not solve this problem either, as the requirements are not OS-agnostic.

The closest you can get locally is by using a Databricks Runtime image in combination with development containers. Even then, the Python environment will not be identical, as Databricks adds additional components that cannot be reproduced outside of the platform.

Fortunately, Databricks developer tools are quite mature today. As an alternative to running notebooks interactively, you can wrap a notebook as a job with specified compute and dependencies and execute it using the databricks bundle run <job-resource-name> command. We will go through this approach in Chapter 5 (for classical ML) and Chapter 9 (for LLM-based applications).

Conclusion

In this chapter, we went through the cluster configurations, the project setup, best practices, and different ways of developing on Databricks. We also showed you some alternatives to developing in a Databricks notebook. But even if you use notebooks, there are some steps you can take that will reduce time to production in the future:

  • Refactor your code into functions and create classes. Structuring code using classes can make the codebase more organized, readable, and modular. With classes, you can bundle class attributes and methods (class functions) into a single unit. You should also separate the data loading, processing, and output steps. This will make the code easier to test and modify.

  • Move code to separate modules. Create a new module for each set of classes. This will make your codebase more modular and reusable. It will also keep your repository nice and tidy and well organized.

  • Package your code. Treat every Python project as a package and specify all the project dependencies and tool configurations in the pyproject.toml file.

  • Create a configuration file or module (like the project_config.yaml file) to store hyperparameters and settings. Keeping configuration settings separate from the main code will allow you to easily adjust the parameters without modifying the main code. It will also be easier to create test scenarios with different configuration settings.

  • Add logging to provide a detailed record of what happens during the execution of your program. When errors or unexpected behavior occur, these logs can help you diagnose and debug issues.

  • Test your code to “fail fast” so you can avoid facing issues in the middle of running your code.
